build_plan.exit_criteria: The disc measures 34.0 mm across and 5.0 mm tall with its top edge rounded 0.6 mm and its underside flat at Z = 0; the seven-segment 4 stands 0.45 mm off the front wall and reads as a 4 in a front elevation; the seat spreads outward from the globe to the disc face. check_overhang finds no region needing support at 45 degrees, which an undrafted numeral and a tangent sphere both fail.

The globe is a full 21.08 mm sphere with nothing cut out of it, and the polar ice stands 1.0 mm proud with a rim that reaches a different latitude at nearly every longitude rather than ending on a circle of latitude. check_mesh returns watertight, manifold and one shell on the fused body.

Land and dryland stand 1.0 mm proud of the ocean, no landmass is narrower than 14 degrees of arc, nothing reaches below latitude 38 S, and each named group is exactly one body. check_thickness passes at a 0.4 mm nozzle with no region classed as a thin wall, and the colour groups sum in volume to the single printed body exactly.

components.duty: Carries the footprint, the weight and the rank. This is the part a player's fingers take hold of, and the numeral is what they read across the board.
components.form: A plain cylinder 34.0 mm across and 5.0 mm tall, its top edge rounded 0.6 mm and its bottom edge square so the piece sits flat. Its front wall carries a seven-segment 4, 2.8 mm wide by 3.6 mm tall, four bars 1.0 mm thick standing 0.45 mm proud. Every bar is drafted: the underside rises 1.2 mm per mm of relief so it is not a ceiling over open air, the sides and top draft 0.5 mm per mm so each face catches light at its own angle.
components.interfaces: Its top face carries the ocean seat. The numeral is fused into the wall, not a separate print.

concept.interaction: A player picks the piece up by its disc base, reads the rank numeral on the wall from a seated position across the board, and sets it down on a square. That is the whole interaction: this is the rank-4 chessman of the matter side and it does exactly what the Dou Shou Qi piece it stands in for does, moving one square orthogonally and capturing an adjacent enemy of equal or lower rank. Nothing on it turns, opens, or comes apart. What the hand gets that a printed ball would not is ground: the continental relief and the polar ice stand a full millimetre off the ocean, so the coastlines can be found by thumb as well as by eye, and the rank numeral stands off the disc wall so the rank can be read by touch in the same grip that lifts the piece.
concept.one_line: A play-scale Dou Shou Qi rank-4 piece: a stylised Earth standing on a flat blue disc that reads 4 in seven bars.
concept.pitch: Dou Shou Qi - matter and antimatter theme: the animal ranks become celestial bodies, and rank four on the matter side is the Earth on its disc.
concept.reskin_claim: Nothing about play changes. This piece is the rank-4 chessman of the matter side: same single rank number, same one-square orthogonal move, same capture relation against ranks at or below it, same board square footprint. The theme replaces the animal with a celestial body and replaces the animal name with a numeral a player can read from a seated position.
concept.scope: The Wish calls this an engineering test run and asks for exactly one piece of the set, not the board, not the opposing faction, and not the remaining ranks. Nothing here claims the rest of the set exists.
concept.signature_promise: Ground you can feel. The continents are raised a real millimetre off the ocean, so the piece is read by thumb as well as by eye, and the rank numeral is raised on the disc wall where a seated player looks.
concept.source_game: Dou Shou Qi, also called Jungle or Jungle Chess
concept.source_rank: Rank 4 in the standard ladder Elephant 8, Lion 7, Tiger 6, Leopard 5, Wolf 4, Dog 3, Cat 2, Rat 1
concept.summary: The rank-four piece of the matter side of Planet Shear: a stylised Earth standing on a flat blue disc whose wall reads 4 in seven raised bars. One printed body, 34.0 mm across the base and 25.08 mm tall, sized to stand in a board square rather than on a shelf.
concept.title: Planet Shear Earth

design_changes.changed: Central America and the Indonesian arc
design_changes.to: one broad land bridge, and no Indonesian arc at all
design_changes.why: On a 21.08 mm globe a degree of arc is 0.184 mm, and a south-facing relief edge needs about seven degrees of ramp to print without support. A landmass under about fourteen degrees wide loses its whole upper face to that ramp.

design_changes.from: a sphere tangent to the disc face, as the reference image composes it
design_changes.to: the globe sunk 2.0 mm with a 25-degree conical ice seat up to latitude 42 S
design_changes.why: A sphere resting tangentially on a plane leaves 189 mm2 of unsupported down-facing surface under it, measured by check_overhang. The seat is finished as the Antarctic ice shelf, which is what the reference shows at that junction anyway.

design_changes.changed: the ice at the foot of the globe
design_changes.from: an ice shelf and a band of southern ice, as the reference image shows
design_changes.to: no ice at the foot at all; the seat is finished in the ocean's own blue
design_changes.why: White there faces downward, shades to mid grey, and two independent review rounds read it as bare unpainted material rather than as ice. A parallel band read as turned on a lathe; ragged tongues read as unfinished. Removing it was worth more than the reference detail it stood in for.

design_changes.from: a cone tucking inward from the globe down to the disc
design_changes.to: a cone spreading outward to the disc face
design_changes.why: Tucking in made the front silhouette pinch above the plate, which an independent reviewer read as the sphere being truncated. Spreading reads as a ball seated on a plate. The sphere itself is untouched at 21.08 mm; the seat is material added around its foot.

design_changes.from: every wall near a leaning one borrowed part of the lean
design_changes.to: a wall facing north borrows none
design_changes.why: A lean is only ever needed where the outline faces south. Borrowed sideways it pushes the top of the patch out past its base: a sub-millimetre undercut lip over the ocean, which an independent reviewer called out as a chip risk on a handled piece and as the relief appearing to lift clear of the sphere.

design_changes.from: the cap's own circle of latitude
design_changes.to: six lobes carrying the ice to a different latitude at nearly every longitude
design_changes.why: An exact parallel is a straight line across the top of the globe in a front elevation and reads as a lid laid on it. Two other repairs were tried and reverted: notches bitten out of the rim made the cap read as a cog, and leaning the cap cone off the polar axis left slivers where it grazed a lobe, which check_mesh caught as five open edges in the printed body.

engineering_findings: A sphere tangent to a flat disc fails check_overhang with a single 189 mm2 unsupported region; a 25-degree conical seat covering the globe past latitude 42 S clears it.

Raised relief on a sphere is a down-facing ledge exactly where the patch outline's outward normal points south and |north component| x cos(latitude) exceeds cos 45. Leaning every wall from one cone apex fixes that and leaves thin cantilevered lips along the diagonal coastlines; leaning each outline vertex by the smallest amount its own boundary needs fixes it without lips.
The rank numeral needs a drafted stroke: an undersized flat-bottomed boss on the wall is a ceiling over open air and fails the overhang gate at 1.1 mm2.

Leaning a cone of revolution off the polar axis to break a rim is not safe here: where the leaned cone grazes a lofted lobe it leaves a sliver, and the fused body comes out with open edges. Breaking the rim by unioning more lobes is sound.

inventor_baseline.why_overridden: The baseline's piece layer is read off a display-scale chess set. This set is play scale, and the Wish fixes the disc at 34.0 mm by 5.0 mm under a 21.08 mm sphere. The baseline itself states every value in it is an overridable default.

reference_image.measurement_note: No dimension was taken from the image. The Wish states the four hard dimensions and forbids re-deriving them.
reference_image.not_observed: The Pacific face of the globe and the rear of the disc wall are absent from the reference and are reconstructed, not matched.
reference_image.observed: One three-quarter front view. A flat circular disc in deep blue with a softened top edge; a blue-ocean globe resting on it; continents in olive green with tan desert across north Africa, Arabia and inner Asia; white ice at the north pole and a ragged white band where the globe meets the disc; a small raised seven-segment 4 centred on the front of the disc wall; the Atlantic face toward the viewer, Americas left, Africa and Europe right.

source_rules.claim: Dou Shou Qi is an old Chinese two-player game played on a 9x7 board; ranks run Elephant 8 down to Rat 1, so rank 4 is the Wolf. Pieces move one square orthogonally and capture an adjacent enemy of equal or lower rank, with the Rat/Elephant exception, rivers, traps and dens.
source_rules.limit: These were read for the rank ladder and the piece's role only. This Make stage did not re-run Mara's broad-popularity or public-domain qualification for the source game: the Wish named Dou Shou Qi, and the host accepted that Wish before this stage started. Nothing here should be read as that qualification having been performed.
